{{Elections in Oregon}}The '''2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Oregon''' were held on November 8, 2022, to elect the six [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] from the [[U.S. state|state]] of [[Oregon]], one from each of the state's six [[Oregon's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. Primaries for these seats were held on May 17, 2022. The elections coincided with the elections and primaries of other federal and state offices.

District boundaries were redrawn<ref>{{cite web|last1=Hammond |first1=Betsy |last2=Friesen |first2=Mark |date=October 3, 2021|title=Map: Look up how partisan your new legislative, congressional districts are in Oregon|url=https://www.oregonlive.com/data/2021/10/map-look-up-how-partisan-your-new-legislative-congressional-districts-are-in-oregon.html|access-date=October 9, 2021|website=[[The Oregonian]] |language=en}}</ref> to ensure that the districts are [[United States congressional apportionment|apportioned]] based on data from the [[2020 United States census]], which added a sixth seat to Oregon's delegation.<ref name=opb/> Democrats won the new sixth district, but Republicans gained Oregon's fifth district, leaving the congressional delegation with a four to two party split in favor of the Democrats. This was the first time since [[1994 United States House of Representatives elections#Oregon|1994]] that Republicans won more than one House seat in Oregon.

{{toclimit|3}}

== Redistricting ==
Ahead of the 2022 elections, Oregon redrew its congressional districts as part of the [[2020 United States redistricting cycle]]. Oregon gained a sixth congressional district during this cycle.<ref name="opb" /> On September 20, 2021, the [[Oregon State Senate]] passed new congressional maps that were favored by Democrats on a party-line vote, along with state legislative maps.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cline |first=Sara |date=September 20, 2021 |title=Oregon Senate passes Dems' redistricting plan as debate begins |url=https://www.columbian.com/news/2021/sep/20/oregon-senate-passes-dems-redistricting-plan-as-debate-begins/ |access-date=January 17, 2024 |website=The Columbian |language=en-US}}</ref> The congressional map contained five Democratic-leaning districts and one Republican-leaning district. [[Tina Kotek]], the Democratic speaker of the [[Oregon House of Representatives]], had negotiated a deal with Republicans to give them equal say on redistricting matters, but she abandoned the deal after the Senate passed its maps.<ref>{{Cite web |last=VanderHart |first=Dirk |date=September 20, 2021 |title=Oregon House Speaker Tina Kotek pulls back on redistricting deal |url=https://www.opb.org/article/2021/09/20/after-slow-start-redistricting-proposals-get-moving-in-salem/ |access-date=January 17, 2024 |website=Oregon Public Broadcasting |language=en}}</ref> House Democrats made changes to the proposed congressional map that made it less favorable towards Democrats, but Republicans still opposed the map. In response, House Republicans skipped a floor session, which denied House Democrats a [[quorum]] and blocked them from being able to pass their maps.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borrud |first=Hillary |date=September 26, 2021 |title=Oregon lawmakers running out of time on redistricting |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/politics/2021/09/oregon-lawmakers-running-out-of-time-on-redistricting.html |access-date=January 17, 2024 |website=The Oregonian |language=en}}</ref> On September 27, the legislature's deadline to approve new maps, most House Republicans showed up to vote. The House's proposed congressional map passed the House and Senate on party-line votes, and was approved by governor [[Kate Brown]] the same day.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borrud |first=Hillary |date=September 27, 2021 |title=Oregon's redistricting maps official, after lawmakers pass them, Gov. Kate Brown signs off |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/politics/2021/09/oregon-legislature-passes-new-legislative-and-congressional-redistricting-plans-sends-to-gov-kate-brown-for-signature.html |access-date=January 17, 2024 |website=The Oregonian |language=en}}</ref>

{{see also|Oregon's 1st congressional district}}
From 2012 to 2020, the 1st district was located in northwestern Oregon and included the western [[Portland metropolitan area|Portland metro area]], including the [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] suburbs of [[Beaverton, Oregon|Beaverton]] and [[Hillsboro, Oregon|Hillsboro]], and parts of Portland west of the [[Willamette River]]. The district was kept largely the same despite redistricting, exchanging [[Yamhill County, Oregon|Yamhill County]] for [[Tillamook County, Oregon|Tillamook County]] and taking in more of Portland. The incumbent was Democrat [[Suzanne Bonamici]], who was re-elected with 64.6% of the vote in 2020.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|Oregon's 2nd congressional district}}
From 2012 to 2020, the 2nd district was the largest of Oregon's districts and covered roughly two-thirds of the state east of the [[Cascade Range|Cascades]], encompassing the [[Central Oregon|central]], [[East Oregon|eastern]], and [[Southern Oregon|southern]] regions of the state, including [[Bend, Oregon|Bend]] and [[Medford, Oregon|Medford]]. The incumbent was Republican [[Cliff Bentz]], who was elected with 59.9% of the vote in 2020.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|Oregon's 3rd congressional district}}
From 2012 to 2020, the 3rd district encompassed the eastern [[Portland metropolitan area|Portland metro area]], covering [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] and [[Gresham, Oregon|Gresham]]. The district was kept largely the same despite redistricting, though it did take in Hood River County, and lost some of Portland to the 1st district. The incumbent was Democrat [[Earl Blumenauer]], who was re-elected with 73.0% of the vote in 2020.<ref name="HPVT"/>

From 2012 to 2020, the 4th district included the southern [[Willamette Valley]] and the [[Southern Oregon Coast|South Coast]], including [[Eugene, Oregon|Eugene]], [[Corvallis, Oregon|Corvallis]], and [[Roseburg, Oregon|Roseburg]]. The district was kept largely the same despite redistricting, though it did gain parts of the central coast previously in the 5th district, making the district more Democratic leaning. The incumbent, Democrat [[Peter DeFazio]], who was re-elected with 51.5% of the vote in 2020,<ref name="HPVT"/> decided to retire, rather than seek a 19th consecutive term in Congress.<ref name="DeFazio"/>

{{see also|Oregon's 5th congressional district}}
From 2012 to 2020, the 5th district straddled the central coast, and included [[Salem, Oregon|Salem]] and the southern [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] suburbs. The new 5th district keeps the southern suburbs of Portland and reaches further into the city, but does not include any coastline, instead stretching southwards through the eastern parts of [[Marion County, Oregon|Marion]] and [[Linn County, Oregon|Linn]] counties to [[Bend, Oregon|Bend]].

The incumbent, Democrat [[Kurt Schrader]], was re-elected with 51.9% of the vote in 2020.<ref name="HPVT">{{cite web|last1=Wasserman|first1=David|last2=Andrews|first2=Sophie|last3=Saenger|first3=Leo|last4=Cohen|first4=Lev|last5=Flinn|first5=Ally|last6=Tatarsky|first6=Griff|title=2020 House Popular Vote Tracker|url=https://cookpolitical.com/2020-house-vote-tracker|publisher=Cook Political Report|access-date=May 10, 2021}}</ref> He lost renomination to [[Jamie McLeod-Skinner]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Centrist Schrader ousted in Oregon primary |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/centrist-schrader-ousted-in-oregon-primary/ar-AAXO5a9 |access-date=May 27, 2022 |website=MSN |language=en-US}}</ref>
